title: Choosing the Right Data Structure

steps.title: Match the structure to the operation
steps.content: Data structures organize information so common operations are efficient. Consider how data is accessed, inserted, removed and searched before choosing one.
steps.example: An array is convenient for indexed access; a linked list supports pointer-based insertion when the position is known.

steps.title: Choose for undo history
steps.prompt: Which structure naturally supports undoing the most recent action first?
steps.explanation: A stack is LIFO, so the most recent action is removed first.

steps.title: Use hashing for lookup
steps.content: A hash map stores key-value pairs and is useful when fast lookup by a key is important. A set is useful when membership and uniqueness matter.
steps.example: A set can detect whether an ID has already appeared.

steps.title: Choose for arrival order
steps.prompt: A customer-service system processes requests in the order received. Which structure is appropriate?
steps.explanation: A queue is FIFO and processes the earliest request first.

steps.title: Think about trade-offs
steps.content: Arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, heaps, hash maps and graphs solve different problems. The right structure depends on required operations, data size and ordering constraints.
steps.tip: Do not choose a structure because it is familiar; choose it because its operations fit the task.

questions.prompt: Which structure is best known for direct indexed access?
questions.explanation: Arrays support direct access by index in O(1) time.

questions.prompt: Which structure models first-in, first-out processing?
questions.explanation: A queue removes the oldest inserted element first.

questions.prompt: Which structure is useful for key-to-value lookup?
questions.explanation: A hash map associates keys with values and offers average constant-time lookup.
Choose a structure based on performance needs, operations and input constraints.

learning_objectives: Choose arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, sets and maps by operation needs.
Compare indexed access, insertion, deletion and lookup costs.
Distinguish abstract data types from their implementations.
Justify a structure using constraints and expected operations.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A data structure is the same as an algorithm.
common_misconceptions.correction: A data structure organizes data; an algorithm operates on it.

common_misconceptions.misconception: One structure is best for every task.
common_misconceptions.correction: Trade-offs depend on access pattern, update frequency and ordering needs.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A hash map preserves sorted order.
common_misconceptions.correction: Typical hash maps prioritize key lookup, not sorted iteration.

worked_examples.title: Choose fast indexed access
trace: The operation needs direct indexed access.
An array computes the position directly.
A linked list must traverse nodes.
worked_examples.explanation: Choose arrays when random access is central.

worked_examples.title: Choose FIFO processing
worked_examples.input: Handle support tickets in arrival order
trace: New tickets join at the back.
worked_examples.explanation: The required order determines the abstract data type.

worked_examples.title: Choose frequency counting
trace: Increment its stored count as it appears.
worked_examples.explanation: A map makes frequency counting concise and usually linear on average.

srs_cards.question: What should you remember about Choosing the Right Data Structure?
srs_cards.answer: Choose arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, sets and maps by operation needs. Compare indexed access, insertion, deletion and lookup costs. Distinguish abstract data types from their implementations. Justify a structure using constraints and expected operations.

srs_cards.question: What mistake should you avoid in Choosing the Right Data Structure?
srs_cards.answer: A data structure organizes data; an algorithm operates on it.
